exampleAnswers.title: Finding Equilibrium Points of a System

question.text: \[ \begin{cases} x'(t) = x(t)+y(t) \\[5pt] y'(t) = 2x(t)+2y(t) \end{cases} \] Which of the following gives all equilibrium points of the system of linear differential equations above?
question.explanation:
Writing our system in matrix form, we have \[ \mathbf{x}(t) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \mathbf{x}(t), \] where $\mathbf{x}(t) = \begin{bmatrix} x(t) \\ y(t) \end{bmatrix}.$

The equilibrium (fixed) points of a system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = \mathbf{f}(x,y)$ are the points for which $f(x,y)=\mathbf{0}.$ So, we get the following system of linear equations: \[ \begin{cases} x+y=0 \\[5pt] 2x+2y=0 \end{cases} \]

Notice that the second equation is a multiple of the first one. So, we can disregard the second equation.

From first equation, we get \[ x+y=0 \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad y=-x. \]

Therefore, the equilibrium points are given by \[ \begin{bmatrix} x(t) \\ y(t) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} k \\ -k \end{bmatrix}, \qquad k \in \mathbb{R}. \]

example.title: Finding Equilibrium Points of a System

question.text: \[ \begin{cases} x'(t) = -3x(t)+y(t) \\[5pt] y'(t) = -6x(t)+2y(t) \end{cases} \] Which of the following gives all equilibrium points of the system of linear differential equations above?
question.explanation:
Writing our system in matrix form, we have \[ \mathbf{x}'(t) = \begin{bmatrix} -3 & 1 \\ -6 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \mathbf{x}(t), \] where $\mathbf{x}(t) = \begin{bmatrix} x(t) \\ y(t) \end{bmatrix}.$

The equilibrium (fixed) points of a system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = \mathbf{f}(x,y)$ are the points for which $\mathbf{f}(x,y)=\mathbf{0}.$ So, we get the following system of linear equations: \[ \begin{cases} -3x+y=0 \\[5pt] -6x+2y=0 \end{cases} \]

Notice that the second equation is a multiple of the first one: \[ 2(-3x+y)=-6x+2y, \] so we can disregard the second equation.

From the first equation, we get \[ -3x+y=0 \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad y=3x. \]

Therefore, the equilibrium points are given by \[ \begin{bmatrix} x(t) \\ y(t) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} k \\ 3k \end{bmatrix}, \qquad k \in \mathbb{R}. \]

example.title: Finding Equilibrium Points of a System

question.text: \[ \begin{cases} x'(t) = 4x(t)-2y(t) \\[5pt] y'(t) = 8x(t)-4y(t) \end{cases} \] Which of the following gives an equation of the line in the phase space that contains all equilibrium points of the system above?
question.explanation:
Writing our system in matrix form, we have \[ \mathbf{x}'(t) = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & -2 \\ 8 & -4 \end{bmatrix} \mathbf{x}(t), \] where $\mathbf{x}(t) = \begin{bmatrix} x(t) \\ y(t) \end{bmatrix}.$

The equilibrium (fixed) points of a system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = \mathbf{f}(x,y)$ are the points for which $\mathbf{f}(x,y)=\mathbf{0}.$ So, we get the following system of linear equations: \[ \begin{cases} 4x-2y=0 \\[5pt] 8x-4y=0 \end{cases} \]

Notice that the second equation is a multiple of the first one. So, we can disregard the second equation.

From the first equation, we get \[ 4x-2y=0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad 2x-y=0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad y=2x. \]

Therefore, the equilibrium points are given by \[ \begin{bmatrix} x(t) \\ y(t) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} k \\ 2k \end{bmatrix}, \qquad k \in \mathbb{R}. \]

This determines the line with the equation $y=2x.$

example.title: Finding Equilibrium Points of a System

question.text: \[ \begin{cases} x'(t) = 3x(t)-6y(t) \\[5pt] y'(t) = x(t)-2y(t) \end{cases} \] Which of the following gives all equilibrium points of the system of linear differential equations above?
question.explanation:
Writing our system in matrix form, we have \[ \mathbf{x}'(t) = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -6 \\ 1 & -2 \end{bmatrix} \mathbf{x}(t), \] where $\mathbf{x}(t) = \begin{bmatrix} x(t) \\[2pt] y(t) \end{bmatrix}.$

The equilibrium (fixed) points of a system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = \mathbf{f}(x,y)$ are the points for which $\mathbf{f}(x,y)=\mathbf{0}.$ So, we get the following system of linear equations: \[ \begin{cases} 3x-6y=0 \\[5pt] x-2y=0 \end{cases} \]

Notice that the first equation is a multiple of the second one: \[ 3(x-2y)=3x-6y, \] so we can disregard the first equation.

From the second equation, we get \[ x-2y=0 \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad x=2y. \]

Therefore, the equilibrium points are given by \[ \begin{bmatrix} x(t) \\ y(t) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2k \\ k \end{bmatrix}, \qquad k \in \mathbb{R}. \]

question.explanation:
Writing our system in matrix form, we have \[ \mathbf{x}'(t) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 6 \end{bmatrix} \mathbf{x}(t), \] where $\mathbf{x}(t) = \begin{bmatrix} x(t) \\ y(t) \end{bmatrix}.$

The equilibrium (fixed) points of a system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = \mathbf{f}(x,y)$ are the points for which $\mathbf{f}(x,y)=\mathbf{0}.$ So, we get the following system of linear equations: \[ \begin{cases} x+2y=0 \\[5pt] 3x+6y=0 \end{cases} \]

Notice that the second equation is a multiple of the first one: \[ 3(x+2y)=3x+6y, \] so we can disregard the second equation.

From the first equation, we get \[ x+2y=0 \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad x=-2y. \]

Therefore, the equilibrium points are given by \[ \begin{bmatrix} x(t) \\ y(t) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2k \\ -k \end{bmatrix}, \qquad k \in \mathbb{R}. \]

exampleAnswers.title: Identifying the Phase Portrait of a System With One Zero Eigenvalue

question.text:
\[ \begin{cases} x'(t) = x(t)+y(t) \\[5pt] y'(t) = 3x(t)+3y(t) \end{cases} \] Consider the system of linear differential equations above. The eigenvalues of the system's matrix are $\lambda_1=0$ and $\lambda_2=4,$ for which the corresponding eigenvectors are $\mathbf{v}_1 = [-1, \ 1]^T$ and $\mathbf{v}_2 = [1, \ 3]^T,$ respectively. Which of the following could represent the phase portrait of the system?

Hint: Here, the dotted line represents the equilibrium solutions.
question.explanation:
The general solution of the system is \[ \mathbf{x}(t)= \begin{bmatrix} x(t)\\y(t)\end{bmatrix} = c_1 \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} + c_2 e^{4t} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad c_1,c_2 \in \mathbb{R}. \]

Let's now sketch the phase portrait.

  • First, notice that $\mathbf{x}_E(t) = c_1 \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$ are the equilibrium solutions of the system since $\mathbf{x}'_E(t) = \mathbf{0}.$ These solutions form the line with the equation $y=-x$ in the phase space, as shown below.
  • Now, the line that passes through the origin and is parallel to $\mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}$ has the equation $ y= 3x $ and the straight-line solutions of the form $ c_2 e^{4t} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix} $ lie on that line. Since $e^{4t} \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty,$ these solutions approach infinity as $t \to \infty.$

All other non-equilibrium solutions are parallel to the vector $\mathbf{v}_2.$ So, the phase portrait of our system looks as follows:

exampleAnswers.title: Identifying the Phase Portrait of a System With Repeated Zero Eigenvalue

question.text:
\[ \begin{cases} x'(t) = 4x(t)-8y(t) \\[5pt] y'(t) = 2x(t)-4y(t) \end{cases} \] Consider the system of linear differential equations above. The eigenvector corresponding to the only eigenvalue $\lambda=0$ of the system's matrix $A$ is $\mathbf{v} = [2, \ 1]^T.$ The vector $\mathbf{w} = \left[\dfrac12, 0\right]^T$ is such that $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{w}= \mathbf{v}.$ Which of the following could represent the phase portrait of the system?

Hint: Here, the dotted line represents the equilibrium solutions.
question.explanation:
Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda=0$ (of multiplicity two) and only one corresponding eigenvector $\mathbf{v},$ the solution of the system is given by \[ \mathbf{x}(t) = c_1\mathbf{v} e^{\lambda t} + c_2 (\mathbf{v} te^{\lambda t} + \mathbf{w}e^{\lambda t} \, ), \] where $\mathbf{w}$ is a solution to the equation $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{w}= \mathbf{v}.$

In our case, \[ \lambda = 0, \qquad \mathbf{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{w} = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac12 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}. \] Thus, the general solution of the system is \begin{align*} \begin{bmatrix} x(t)\\y(t)\end{bmatrix} &= c_1 \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} + c_2 \left( \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} t + \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac12 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \right) \\[5pt] &= c_1 \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} + c_2 \begin{bmatrix} 2t+\dfrac12 \\ t \end{bmatrix}, \qquad c_1,c_2 \in \mathbb{R}. \end{align*}

First, notice that $\mathbf{x}_E(t) = c_1 \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$ are equilibrium solutions of the system since $\mathbf{x}'_E(t) = \mathbf{0}.$ These solutions form the line with the equation $y=\dfrac12x$ in the phase space, as shown below.

Now, we consider some general solutions of the form \[ \begin{bmatrix} x(t)\\y(t)\end{bmatrix} = c_1 \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} + c_2 \begin{bmatrix} 2t+\dfrac12 \\ t \end{bmatrix}. \] For example:

  • When $c_1=1$ and $c_2=2,$ we get the following curve: \[ \begin{cases} x = 4t+3 \\[3pt] y = 2t+1 \end{cases} \] Let's add it to the phase space:
  • When $c_1=-1$ and $c_2=-2,$ we get the following curve: \[ \begin{cases} x = -4t-3 \\[3pt] y = -2t-1 \end{cases} \]

Let's add it to the phase space:

The phase portrait of our system looks as follows:

\[ \begin{cases} x'(t) = x(t)-y(t) \\[5pt] y'(t) = x(t)-y(t) \end{cases} \] Consider the system of linear differential equations above. The eigenvector corresponding to the only eigenvalue $\lambda=0$ of the system's matrix $A$ is $\mathbf{v} = [1, \ 1]^T.$ The vector $\mathbf{w} = [1, \ 0]^T$ is such that $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{w}= \mathbf{v}.$ Which of the following could represent the phase portrait of the system?

Hint: Here, the dotted line represents the equilibrium solutions.
question.explanation:
Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda=0$ (of multiplicity two) and only one corresponding eigenvector $\mathbf{v},$ the solution of the system is given by \[ \mathbf{x}(t) = c_1\mathbf{v} e^{\lambda t} + c_2 (\mathbf{v} te^{\lambda t} + \mathbf{w}e^{\lambda t} \, ), \] where $\mathbf{w}$ is a solution to the equation $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{w}= \mathbf{v}.$

In our case, \[ \lambda = 0, \qquad \mathbf{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{w} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}. \] Thus, the general solution of the system is \begin{align*} \begin{bmatrix} x(t)\\y(t)\end{bmatrix} &= c_1 \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} + c_2 \left( \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} t + \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \right) \\[5pt] &= c_1 \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} + c_2 \begin{bmatrix} t+1 \\ t \end{bmatrix}, \qquad c_1,c_2 \in \mathbb{R}. \end{align*}

First, notice that $\mathbf{x}_E(t) = c_1 \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$ are equilibrium solutions of the system since $\mathbf{x}'_E(t) = \mathbf{0}.$ These solutions form the line with the equation $y=x$ in the phase space, as shown below.

Now, we consider some general solutions of the form \[ \begin{bmatrix} x(t)\\y(t)\end{bmatrix} = c_1 \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} + c_2 \begin{bmatrix} t+1 \\ t \end{bmatrix}. \] For example:

  • When $c_1=1$ and $c_2=1,$ we get the following curve: \[ \begin{cases} x = 2t+2 \\[3pt] y = 2t+1 \end{cases} \] Let's add it to the phase space:
  • When $c_1=-1$ and $c_2=-1,$ we get the following curve: \[ \begin{cases} x = -2t-2 \\[3pt] y = -2t-1 \end{cases} \] Let's add it to the phase space:
